body.text: It used to be relatively rare to hear or see the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) publicize its vulnerabilities or engage in self-criticism. Yet, in the closing communique issued after the fifth plenum – the CCP’s recent four-day meeting from October 26 to 29 – the failings of party leadership were openly highlighted, along with the naming and shaming of dozens of members in CCP and military leadership. The very public purge is part of an ongoing anti-corruption campaign that Xi Jinping has pursued since his ascension to the top spot of general secretary of the CCP in 2012.
By releasing the communique to Xinhua, China’s official state news agency, for dissemination to the wider public, Xi becomes the hero of his own story.

“It was unanimously agreed,” the communique said, “that the Central Committee with Comrade Xi Jinping at its core demonstrated tremendous political courage and a strong sense of responsibility in confronting the grave situation marked by weak, hollow, and watered-down party leadership, lax, superficial, and ineffective self-supervision and self-governance, as well as some startling problems within the party.”

Under Xi’s leadership, these problems have been “addressed at the root,” the report continued, and “unhealthy tendencies that had long gone unchecked have been curbed, deep-seated problems that had plagued the party for years have been remedied, and serious dangers hidden within the party, the state, and the military have been removed.”

The heavy flattery is especially interesting as, according to the South China Morning Post, “Xi revealed that he personally led the high-profile drafting team starting in early February 2026, working alongside Politburo Standing Committee members Wang Huning, Cai Qi, and anti-corruption chief Li Xi.”

The communique wants to make two key and crucial points at the same time. One, the CCP emphasized that there have been major operational, governance, and supervisory problems in the party for years. In the interest of openness, the communique admitted this. But, it hastened to add, many of those issues are now resolved, thanks in large part to Xi.

And yet, it seems that corruption remains an ongoing issue. After all, the fifth plenum and its resulting major resolution are meant to spell out to party cadres and leadership alike that investigations and disciplinary measures are not only going to continue but will indeed increase as needed.

According to the Global Times, an English-language paper under the umbrella of the official CCP mouthpiece, People’s Daily, the resolution paves the way to “reinforcing Xi Jinping’s core status and emphasizing strict ideological and political loyalty within the party.”

Ultimately, according to the communique, the CCP must rely upon self-governance and no other method of governing as the means of leading and developing China. As such, the plenum adopted the awkwardly-titled “Resolution on Certain Major Issues concerning Persevering with Full and Rigorous Party Self-Governance.”

“The experts stressed that the greatest threats to a ruling party can come from within, making sustained self-governance and strict internal discipline essential to avoiding the historical cycle of rise and decline,” the Global Times reported. Indeed, “self-governance” appears 31 times in the 10-page report.

In other words – and the communique doubles down on this point – China today by its very design and definition is a one-party state, and the CCP has no intentions of changing or reforming that condition. Quite the opposite.

This is hardly the first time that Chinese officialdom has publicly addressed the subject of governance of and in China. It is worth revisiting an April 14, 2022, report originally written by the Office of the Central National Security Commission. Titled “Uphold the Predominant Position of Political Security,” the report foretold many of the points of this year’s plenum communique, but in often blunter terms.

“It is erroneous, harmful, and unconstitutional for any person to repudiate the leadership of the Chinese Communist Party and our socialist institutions under any pretext. No one who behaves in such a manner will be tolerated,” read the report.
The document continued

It is necessary to unwaveringly uphold and strengthen the party’s leadership and governing status. Our regime rests on Chinese Communist Party rule, with the consultative participation of various democratic parties. There are no opposition parties. There is no separation of powers between three branches [of government], with multiple parties taking turns to rule. The Constitution of our state affirms the ruling position of the Chinese Communist Party. It affirms the party’s place as the core of the political power structure, coordinating the various parts with total authority over the greater whole. The party leads all.
That last line may make some people shiver.

Xi’s program of purging corrupt party members rests to a large degree upon the political and ideological concepts of the “four tests” and the “four dangers.” The communique acknowledged their importance: “[T]he ‘four tests’ and ‘four dangers’ confronting our party are still protracted, complicated, and serious.”
Although Xi Jinping has amplified the “four tests” and “four dangers” concepts, in fact it was his predecessor, Hu Jintao, who in 2011 initially created the paradigm.

The first of the “four tests” that the CCP must pass is the test of governing – maintaining legitimacy, and the public’s support for the CCP’s long-term right to rule, while remaining administratively effective. Second is the rest of “reform and opening.” The CCP must manage the huge social, economic, and cultural changes that come with globalization and market liberalization. Third, and related, is the “market economy” test. The CCP must navigate the corrupting and destabilizing influences of a market-driven economy while maintaining state control. Fourth, and finally, the “external environment.” The CCP must manage geopolitical pressures, shifts in international relations, and challenges from external ideological and security situations, all without jeopardizing China’s internal stability (meaning, in the party’s eyes, its own absolute control).

The “four tests” involve conditions that the CCP must respond to. By contrast, the “four dangers” all come from within. These are internal threats that could weaken or destroy the party if left unchecked: loss of vitality (including ideological stagnation, loss of revolutionary zeal, and bureaucratic inertia), insufficient capacity (including a lack of modern governing skills and sheer incompetence in and of itself), alienation from the people (growing detachment, arrogance, or loss of close ties between party cadres and the general public), and finally, the existence of rampant corruption, widespread bribery, abuse of power, and moral decay.
A full 15 years after Hu Jintao unveiled the concept, the CCP is still fighting the same battles.

In Xi Jinping’s explanatory note for the resolution, he reiterated that the plenum’s theme of self-governance “is an ‘inevitable requirement’ to preserve ideological purity. It is also necessary in order to prevent corruption from eroding the party, and to ensure the party’s hold on power.”

Xi did not explain, however, how his party can continue to claim total legitimacy in the face of having exposed millions of party cadres, from top to bottom, who have abused their office and CCP membership for personal gain. Some of the corruption occurred during the rule of Xi’s predecessors, to be sure, but the party was the same party as today.

One final note: A significant number of seats were empty during the meetings. Therefore, it is worth noting that calling this meeting a “plenum” may be a bit of a misnomer. According to the Cambridge Dictionary, a plenum in politics and governance is “a meeting at which all the members of a group or organization are present.” That didn’t happen this year.
Indeed, as Think China pointed out:

The plenum was attended by 162 full Central Committee members and 117 alternate members, or 279 people in total. That figure equals 74.2 percent of the 205 full members and alternate members elected at the 20th Party Congress in 2022. Compared with the fourth plenum in October 2025, attendance by full members declined by six and attendance by alternate members fell by 30. The published figures are attendance figures rather than an exact measure of the number of serving members, but they nevertheless mark an unusually low level by recent standards.

The overall tone of the communique serves as a stark and dark warning to CCP members, officials, and the military, that there is no rest or reprieve ahead for those who may have flouted party rules and regulations. Xi’s crusade is likely to have advanced even further into the depths of party misbehavior by the time the party meets again in the second half of 2027 for the all-important 21st National Party Congress, which will cement CCP leadership for the next five years. Either way, a challenge to Xi’s continued leadership may be in the offing. He has his supporters, to be sure, but through his purges, he has also made enemies, many of them.
